extracted.intended_audience: middle- and upper-class women, parents, and general readers seeking guidance on social manners and personal hygiene
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on personal veracity, social conventionalities, intimacy boundaries, child-rearing of manners, and bodily hygiene/diet—presented as practical rules and examples for well-bred individuals (especially women and mothers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / Veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the truth; avoid exaggeration, invention, or allowing imagination to supply missing facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the misheard medical story: fragments gleaned from conversation can be unconsciously embroidered into falsehoods. Cultivate veracity as a virtue; prune loose statements. Antipatterns: producing 'romances constructed upon the impressionist-picture plan' or allowing the desire to produce a sensation to distort facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'too frank' impertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from uttering unnecessary and unkind criticisms even if sincere; being 'nothing if not candid' is not true politeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unsolicited remarks about another's gown, hair, or household management are impertinent. One may be truthful without bestowing gratuitous advice and admonition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let family rows or private faults be publicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep family matters private; do not discuss or expose the faults, peccadilloes, or shortcomings of family members to outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxim: 'wash her dirty linen at home.' Whether a relative is hypocrite, fool, or worse, if you pretend to be on speaking terms, stand up for them; if relations are severed, still avoid broadcasting faults for politeness and self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children must be trained by example in honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents and elders must guard their own speech because children quickly detect and imitate insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If children inherit insincerity, it's hard to correct; watch children from infancy, correct exaggeration, and be absolutely truthful to inspire confidence. Antipattern: mother who lies to preserve social reputation then punishes child for lying.

rubrics_metrics.name: When telling a story, reduce rather than exaggerate
rubrics_metrics.description: If you err in telling a wonderful story, prefer cutting details rather than magnifying them—'a couple of ciphers less are better than one too many.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves honesty and prevents the habit of embellishment that degrades taste for proportion and right coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and maintain conventionalities ('the Gospel of Conventionalities')
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional manners and usages (etiquette) are valuable: they beautify life and often have hygienic or social-utility reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventionalities may promote hygiene or the greatest good to the greatest number; rejecting them shows self-conceit. Antipattern: obstinate refusal to adopt reasonable refinements because 'my parents did without them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish and finish (cultivate refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: External polish should be durable and rest on sound underlying material—true refinement is judged by intimacy and durability under scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy of carriage finishing: varnish alone is worthless on poor material. Inner refinement should prevent familiarity that breeds contempt. Antipattern: superficial polish that flakes under stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the 'bread-and-butter' thank-you note promptly after a visit
rubrics_metrics.description: After visiting a hostess (even for one night), send a brief note as soon as possible informing her of safe arrival and thanking her for hospitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few lines are sufficient; this is a small token of courtesy expected in decent society.

rubrics_metrics.name: When entering a hostess's drawing-room, seek the hostess first
rubrics_metrics.description: On entering a parlor full of people, do not stop to speak to acquaintances before finding and paying respects to the entertainer (host/hostess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If addressed en route, make an apology and pass on until you have greeted the hostess; after that you are free to converse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe precedence and public courtesies (e.g., give lady the chair)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not arrogantly refuse accepted rules of courtesy such as yielding a chair to a lady in crowded rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many small tokens of good breeding (table and parlor manners, dress, visiting etiquette) are often neglected but important for social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not enter a friend's house or private room unannounced
rubrics_metrics.description: Always ring the bell to enter a friend's house and knock before entering private rooms—even familiar friends must respect privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country 'running in' annoys busy housekeepers; entering bed-chamber or sanctum without knocking is an unwarrantable rudeness. When two people share a chamber, it remains private: others must knock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offering unsolicited advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Give opinions only when asked; unsolicited judgment implicates you unnecessarily in others' affairs and is usually unwelcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: correcting another person's child in the parent's presence or intervening in private discipline. Lawyers' practice of declining to advise unless paid is used as an analogy for restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct children privately, not in front of parents or third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Never reprimand another person's child in the presence of the child's parents; this is impertinent and insulting to parental authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: visitor reproofs Johnny while mother is present; grandparent intervenes before mother—both provoke resentment in child and parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive questions about finances or private matters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is bad breeding to ask 'feelers' about another's income, prices paid, mortgages, rent, or household costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper queries: 'How much did you pay for that horse?' 'Have you a mortgage?' Such questions may tempt the restrained person to lose composure; labeled 'None of your blamed business.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Table etiquette: observe established rules and avoid improprieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Know and follow table customs; do not ask household staff for inappropriate items or display ignorance of basic table manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of breaches: a guest asking the hostess to order mustard or requesting butler bring a glass of milk—indicates lack of early parental admonition and polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proper boundaries of familiarity vs intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume intimacy: avoid physical familiarity (slaps on back, squeezing arm, holding hands too long) or using first names publicly without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a male friend drops courteous forms of address without permission, he shows lack of respect and should be dropped as an intimate. A 'finished' person won't presume this concession gives license to remove titles from you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful referencing of people (use proper forms of address)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true gentleman does not speak of a lady to strangers without her 'handle' (title); women should not refer to men only by last names as evidence of poor polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a woman speaks of 'Smith,' 'Brown' or 'Jones' without courtesy, it reveals neglect of finishing varnish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show 'small sweet courtesies'—express care by attentive acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make yourself pleasing by showing care for others through little tender acts, looks, and giving preference in small enjoyments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote William Wirt: the world will serve you as you serve others; small unobtrusive courtesies still, ease, and manifest affection (giving others preference at table, walking, sitting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude the 'three D's' from polite conversation: Domestics, Dress, Diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making domestics, dress, and diseases the staple of polite conversation—especially avoid dwelling on illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower classes may 'enjoy poor health' and discuss complaints endlessly; polite society should refrain from such topics. Discussing diseases is gauche and tiresome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care for the stomach: prevention over dosing
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect digestive health by preventive care, sensible diet, and avoiding habitual reliance on medicines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'take a course of physic' as mere principle; if stomach is irritable, soothe rather than punish—use fasting for a few hours, then slowly take light food (milk-toast or hot beef-tea). Avoid becoming dependent on pepsin or bicarbonate of soda; if a food disagrees (hot breads, pastry, fried/greasy food, nuts, sweets), abstain from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of bicarbonate of soda and other habitual remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: While bicarbonate can correct acidity occasionally, large and frequent doses can damage the stomach lining and have produced severe outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: dyspeptics taking soda routinely after each meal—this dependence is cautioned against and may lead to worse conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fasting and light diet to soothe an irritated stomach
rubrics_metrics.description: When digestion is disordered, a few hours' fasting followed by small amounts of light, easily digested food is often better than copious medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested foods: milk-toast, very hot beef-tea. Quiet and diet can work more wonders than quarts of medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain skin cleanliness and keep pores open
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular washing/all-over sponging and the use of soap and warm water keep the skin's pores open to dispose of impurities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponging once a day where perspiration accumulates; frequent plunge baths are recommended to open pores and thoroughly cleanse; partial washing (face/hands only) is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise regularly and abundantly
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular and ample physical exercise is an essential desideratum for bodily health (especially digestive and general hygiene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise complements cleanliness and diet in maintaining the 'system of drains' and general well-being; mentioned as a concluding imperative for care of the stomach and health.
